passages.title: Task 1
passages.text:
(1) When Erdene needed a drill to put up a single shelf, she did not go to a shop. Instead, she went to her local library. Next to the shelves of novels and dictionaries there was a room full of tools, tents, sewing machines and even musical instruments. She borrowed a drill for a week, used it for ten minutes and returned it.

(2) Libraries like this one are sometimes called "libraries of things". Their supporters point out that many household tools are used for only a few minutes a year. "It makes no sense for every family on a street to own a drill that sits in a cupboard all year," says Dulamaa, the librarian who manages the collection. "Sharing saves money, space and resources."

(3) Before opening the collection, the library spent several months asking local people what they would like to borrow. It then compared their answers with lists of the items that people most often threw away or sold second-hand.

(4) The results were sometimes surprising. Few people asked for expensive electronics, but many wanted camping equipment, large cooking pots for family celebrations and tools for small repairs. These now make up most of the collection, and some items are booked for months ahead.

(5) The idea is not perfect. Things break, some are returned late, and someone has to check and clean everything. Even so, the library believes that borrowing instead of buying is a habit worth teaching. As Dulamaa puts it, "A tool on a shelf is a waste. A tool that travels from home to home is a small gift to everyone."
